tracks.label: Web
tracks.note: The programmable web: CGI, mod_perl, PSGI

events.title: Perl 1.0 is posted to Usenet
events.summary: Larry Wall releases Perl 1.0 as a tool sitting between shell scripting and C — report generation, text extraction, and gluing systems together.
events.whyItMattered: It gave sysadmins a single language for the work that previously needed awk, sed, sh and a C program stitched together.
events.whatRemains: The design bias is still visible: regular expressions as a first-class construct, and a bias toward getting the job done over ceremony.

events.title: Programming Perl, first edition
events.summary: The first substantial book on the language ships, alongside Perl 4.
events.whyItMattered: Documentation, not the interpreter, is what let Perl spread into organisations that had never heard of Usenet.
events.whatRemains: The habit of shipping prose with the code — perldoc is still part of the distribution, not an afterthought.

events.title: CGI takes shape around NCSA httpd
events.summary: The Common Gateway Interface convention establishes how a web server hands a request to an external program and reads a response back from standard output.
events.whyItMattered: It made the web writable. Any language that could read environment variables and print to stdout could now serve a dynamic page — and Perl was already on every Unix box.
events.whatRemains: The request/response contract survived the transport. PSGI, WSGI, Rack and Servlet are all recognisably the same idea with a better calling convention.

events.title: Perl 5.000
events.summary: References, modules, packages and a rewritten interpreter core arrive in one release.
events.whyItMattered: Modules made shared code possible, which is the precondition for everything CPAN became a year later.
events.whatRemains: Every `use` statement you write today rests on the package and module system introduced here.

events.title: CPAN goes live
events.summary: Jarkko Hietaniemi brings the Comprehensive Perl Archive Network online as a mirrored, indexed archive of modules and distributions.
events.whyItMattered: It is the first widely used language package archive of its kind, and the template most later ecosystems copied.
events.whatRemains: The mirror network, the author-namespaced distribution model, and the expectation that a language ships with a way to get other people's code.

events.title: mod_perl embeds the interpreter in Apache
events.summary: Doug MacEachern's module puts a persistent Perl interpreter inside the web server process.
events.whyItMattered: It removed the per-request process fork that made CGI slow, and gave Perl access to the server's own request lifecycle.
events.whatRemains: The persistent-process model. Every modern application server — PSGI, WSGI, Rack — assumes the interpreter stays warm between requests.

events.title: Perl 5.004 ships CGI.pm in core
events.summary: Lincoln Stein's CGI.pm becomes part of the standard distribution: parameter parsing, header generation and HTML helpers in one module.
events.whyItMattered: Handwritten form parsers were the single largest source of web security bugs in that era. A shared implementation in core removed a class of them.
events.whatRemains: The interface convention. It also became the reference case for why a batteries-included module can outlive its own good idea — see 2015.

events.title: Perl 6 is announced
events.summary: A redesign of the language is announced at the Perl Conference, driven by community RFCs.
events.whyItMattered: It set two decades of expectations — and, for a long stretch, drained attention from the language people were actually shipping.
events.whatRemains: A hard lesson about naming a successor before it exists. Resolved in 2019 by renaming it Raku and separating the two languages.

events.title: Perl 5.10, on Perl's twentieth birthday
events.summary: Named captures, defined-or, `say`, state variables and a faster regex engine ship exactly twenty years after Perl 1.0.
events.whyItMattered: It ended the assumption that Perl 5 had stopped moving while Perl 6 was designed.
events.whatRemains: `//`, `say` and named captures are ordinary idioms now. So is the annual release cadence that followed.

events.title: PSGI and Plack
events.summary: Tatsuhiko Miyagawa specifies PSGI — a request hashref in, a three-element response arrayref out — and ships Plack as the reference toolkit.
events.whyItMattered: It decoupled Perl web applications from the server that runs them, which is the change CGI.pm-era code never made.
events.whatRemains: Every current Perl web framework speaks PSGI. It is the single most important interface in modern Perl web work.

events.title: Mojolicious 1.0
events.summary: A real-time web framework with no non-core dependencies, a built-in test framework, and a single-file `Mojolicious::Lite` mode.
events.whyItMattered: It made the smallest useful Perl web application a legible twelve-line file again — the thing CGI got right — without the CGI execution model.
events.whatRemains: `Mojolicious::Lite` is still the shortest honest path from an idea to a running HTTP service in Perl.

events.title: Perl 5.22 removes CGI.pm from core
events.summary: After deprecation in 5.20, CGI.pm leaves the standard distribution. It remains installable from CPAN.
events.whyItMattered: Core is a maintenance promise, not a museum. Removing a module that had outlived its execution model was the honest call.
events.whatRemains: A great deal of running code that still `use CGI;` — which is exactly why Script Rescue exists on this site.

events.title: Perl 6 "Christmas" release
events.summary: The first official language release, fifteen years after the announcement.
events.whyItMattered: It converted an open-ended redesign into a finished, versioned language — and made the naming problem impossible to defer.
events.whatRemains: The language, now called Raku. And the clarity that it is a sibling, not a successor.

events.title: Perl 6 is renamed Raku
events.summary: The community accepts a rename, ending nineteen years of a shared name for two different languages.
events.whyItMattered: It let both projects be described accurately for the first time since 2000.
events.whatRemains: Perl means Perl again. When this site says Perl, it means the language that shipped 5.x.

events.title: Perl 5.38 ships an experimental core `class`
events.summary: A native object system enters the language as an experimental feature, alongside the long-established CPAN options.
events.whyItMattered: It is the first serious attempt to answer "which OO system should I use?" from inside the language rather than from CPAN.
events.whatRemains: Still experimental. Treat it as a signal about direction, not as a stable target for production code yet.

events.title: Perl 5.44.0 becomes the current stable release
events.summary: The first production release of the 5.44 series.
events.whyItMattered: It is the stable baseline recommended by perl.org for new installations.
events.whatRemains: Development releases continue on a separate odd-numbered branch; production guidance stays on 5.44.x.

events.title: PerlCoders relaunches as an independent publication
events.summary: New ownership, new editorial scope: practical Perl, honest language comparisons, web-automation tooling, and a properly sourced history.
events.whyItMattered: The trace does not stop. This node stays open.
events.whatRemains: Everything after this is unwritten. Corrections and submissions are how it gets written.
